title: Laxer abbreviations file syntax: ignore rest of line after first space
body:
The manual says that each line in an abbreviations file must contain one abbreviation without whitespace. It would be convenient if you could use space/tabs but the rest of the line after the first space/tab on were ignored. You could then include expansions and/or comments, making files self-documenting. You could even use a format `abbr. : expansion and/or comment` which would be valid YAML!

My use case is that I have a set of Perl scripts which allow me to do certain things with one or more yaml files like described above:

1.  Search keys and/or values for regex/substring matches.
2.  Generate a (sorted) Markdown table or definition list of abbreviations.
3.  Generate a file containing all unique keys/abbreviations as understood by Pandoc.

It would be good to get rid of (3) not because it is a hassle to run the script but because keeping both files updated and in sync is a hassle.

Cf. #8520

body:
<!--

**Describe your proposed improvement and the problem it solves.**

According to the [Manual](https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html), Pandoc has support for plaintext output but not for plaintext input.

With `pandoc -f plain`, a user should be able to explicitly declare that Pandoc should treat the input as plain text.

For example, with `pandoc -t latex <<< "2) Hello world"`, Pandoc will interpret the leading `2) ` as an evidence for ordered list. Without the `-f plain` option, it will be difficult to avoid such error.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2139261/217375015-a3f7090e-719b-4a02-8b14-ab50f1b00c8a.png)


**Describe alternatives you've considered.**

https://github.com/neruthes/NDevShellRC/blob/master/bin/safepandoc

```
#!/bin/bash

#
# safepandoc
#
# Copyright (c) 2023 Neruthes.
# This script is free software, published with GNU GPL 2.0 license.
#

DEST_FORMAT="$1"
if [[ -z "$1" ]]; then
    echo -e "safepandoc (version 0.1.0)
Copyright (c) 2023 Neruthes.
This script is free software, published with GNU GPL 2.0 license.\n
Usage:
    safepandoc {dest_format} <<< 'your input text'
    safepandoc {dest_format} plain-input.txt\n
    This script persuades Pandoc to treat your input as genuine plaintext.
    The list of valid destination formats are availble in Pandoc manual:
        <https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#general-options>
">&2
    exit 0
fi

TMP="/tmp/$(uuidgen v4)"

input_fn="$2"
if [[ -z "$2" ]]; then
    input_fn="/dev/stdin"
fi
cat "$input_fn" > "$TMP.stdin"

FORMATS_LIST="markdown gfm csv tsv org rst jira html latex"

for fmt in $FORMATS_LIST; do
    out_fn="$TMP.$fmt"
    pandoc --wrap=none -i "$TMP.stdin" -o "$out_fn" -f "$fmt" -t plain
    if [[ -z "$(diff "$TMP.stdin" "$out_fn")" ]]; then
        good_fmt="$fmt"
        echo "debug: good_fmt=$good_fmt">&2

done

if [[ -n "$good_fmt" ]]; then
    pandoc --wrap=none -f "$good_fmt" -t "$DEST_FORMAT" -i "$TMP.stdin" && rm "$TMP".*
else
    echo "-----------------------------------------" >&2
    echo "[ERROR] The input is too tricky. Cannot find any possible format.">&2
    cat "$TMP.stdin" >&2
    echo "-----------------------------------------" >&2
    exit 1
fi

title: Provide a `pandoc.json` Lua JSON library
body:
It would be great to have access to pandoc's JSON handlers. Part of this is that JSON support in Lua is slightly opinionated, as there is no default method to represent JSON `null` values: while some libraries use `nil`, others use special table values or C null pointers (as light userdata). Pandoc, when marshaling values via JSON, uses null pointers.

One of the advantages of shipping a JSON library would be that it would use the existing encoding method, avoiding potentially subtle bugs.

Proposed functions:

- `pandoc.json.encode`: converts the given Lua object to JSON. All pandoc *userdata* objects (blocks, inlines, etc) should result in their default JSON encoding. Objects with a `__tojson` metamethod would be encoded by invoking that function.
- `pandoc.json.decode`: the inverse function; tries to decode the JSON as AST element or \*Option value, but falls back to a normal Lua table if that's not possible.
- Field `pandoc.json.null` containing the null pointer as light userdata.

Cc: @cscheid

title: workaround for keeping `th` vs `td` information in a Table through html's table reader
body:
Pandoc (I tried 2.19.2 and 3.1) appears to not keep track of `th` vs `td` elements in table bodies. Consider this example: ```` $ cat pandoc-tables-th.html
12
34
$ pandoc pandoc-tables-th.html
1 2
3 4
```` It seems that Pandoc has a specific opinion on how to support and emit `th` vs `td`. Using `th` in non-standard places is somewhat unusual HTML syntax, but is allowed [by the HTML spec](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/tables.html#the-th-element) and there's good reasons to support it. Specifically, when it comes to accessibility, `th` elements are treated differently by screen readers. **Describe your proposed improvement and the problem it solves.** It would be very useful to track the `th` information inside the Cell elements, so that `th`-in-body tables were possible to produce with Pandoc. (This comes up in quarto because we parse HTML tables and allow Lua filters to operate on the resulting AST.) I think the simplest solution would be to enrich the Cell data type to carry `td` or `th` with it, and make it so that html formats emit those. In addition, the current parser appears to ignore `colspan` attributes in `th` elements in the body: ``` $ cat pandoc-table-body-colspan.html
12
a heading
$ pandoc pandoc-table-body-colspan.html
1 2
a heading
``` Note how we lost the `colspan` in that entry. It doesn't make it to the AST node: ``` $ pandoc pandoc-table-body-colspan.html -t native [ Table ( "" , [] , [] ) (Caption Nothing []) [ ( AlignDefault , ColWidthDefault ) , ( AlignDefault , ColWidthDefault ) ] (TableHead ( "" , [] , [] ) []) [ TableBody ( "" , [] , [] ) (RowHeadColumns 1) [] [ Row ( "" , [] , [] ) [ Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 1) [ Plain [ Str "1" ] ] , Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 1) [ Plain [ Str "2" ] ] ] , Row ( "" , [] , [] ) [ Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 1) [ Plain [ Str "a" , Space , Str "heading" ] ] , Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 1) [] ] ] ] (TableFoot ( "" , [] , [] ) []) ] ``` Notably, `colspan` _is_ supported in the tablehead itself: ``` $ cat pandoc-table-head-colspan.html
a heading
12
$ pandoc pandoc-table-head-colspan.html [ Table ( "" , [] , [] ) (Caption Nothing []) [ ( AlignDefault , ColWidthDefault ) , ( AlignDefault , ColWidthDefault ) ] (TableHead ( "" , [] , [] ) [ Row ( "" , [] , [] ) [ Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 2) [ Plain [ Str "a" , Space , Str "heading" ] ] ] ]) [ TableBody ( "" , [] , [] ) (RowHeadColumns 0) [] [ Row ( "" , [] , [] ) [ Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 1) [ Plain [ Str "1" ] ] , Cell ( "" , [] , [] ) AlignDefault (RowSpan 1) (ColSpan 1) [ Plain [ Str "2" ] ] ] ] ] (TableFoot ( "" , [] , [] ) []) ] ``` **Describe alternatives you've considered.** N/A **Potential issues** I think this might cause a slight bit of backwards incompatibility, because some Pandoc chooses to use th and td in ways that I don't quite understand. My proposed AST change would mean that for an HTML reader, there would be explicit `th` and `td` preservation. The other readers could emit a TH marker for the first cell of a row (or whatever is the relevant Pandoc logic), and so the table HTML output would still be preserved.

**Explain the problem.** Consider the following DocBook document (example.xml): ```xml
My document
``` When converting the above DocBook with pandoc, the AST obtained with `pandoc -f docbook -t native example.xml` is: ```haskell [ Header 1 ( "my-document" , [] , [] ) [ Str "My" , Space , Str "document" ] , Para [ Image ( "my_figure_id" , [] , [] ) [ Str "This" , Space , Str "is" , Space , Str "the" , Space , Str "caption" ] ( "my_image.png" , "fig:" ) ] ] ``` Then, for example, when I convert the DocBook document to LaTeX, the figure is considered to be an inline element and thus a figure environment is not created, i.e., this is the output of `pandoc -f docbook -t latex example.xml`: ```latex \hypertarget{my-document}{% \section{My document}\label{my-document}} \includegraphics{my_image.png} ``` The figure has no caption and no label so it cannot be cross-referenced. Note that the previous examples were obtained with the development version of pandoc. I also tried with pandoc version 2.14.0.3 (the one that is available in the Fedora 37 repositories, the OS that I am currently using) and in that version the result was as expected: the command `pandoc -f docbook -t latex example.xml` produced the following result ```latex \hypertarget{my-document}{% \section{My document}\label{my-document}} \begin{figure} \centering \includegraphics{my_image.png} \caption{This is the caption} \end{figure} ``` This seems to be related to the `Figure` block element discussed in https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/issues/3177. Note that DocBook also has an `informalfigure` element (https://tdg.docbook.org/tdg/5.1/informalfigure.html), this is a figure without title, currently it is processed in the same way as the `figure` element, but the `informalfigure` element is also a block element, thus I guess it should be also converted to a `Figure` element in the pandoc AST. **Pandoc version?** Pandoc development version

title: HTML writer generates duplicate classes on elements & should de-duplicate for clearer HTML
body:
The Pandoc HTML writer will generate duplicate classes on HTML elements; this may combine with Markdown<->HTML roundtrips or API use to lead to some elements like tables having 5+ redundant classes set on an element. While legal HTML and not immediately producing any bugs (because classes are idempotent), this is somewhat dangerous/confusing (and slightly inefficient/ugly), and it would be good if Pandoc could just uniquefy classes. --- My web guy was disconcerted while debugging another issue to see a bunch of HTML table with many instances of the `even`/`odd` class, wondering if there was some bug, eg: ~~~{.HTML} ~~~ (I had noticed these myself but I think I had written them off as some sort of nesting, where 'even even' != 'even', until he explained that *HTML* classes, as opposed to CSS rules, didn't work that way: those were all just equivalent to `class="even"/"odd"` and so why was my HTML weird like that? Was something broken? No, it was fine, just seemed to be Pandoc doing something odd.) I wondered if some Pandoc process was generating multiple instances of a class, but Pandoc is apparently content to pass through any number of classes: ~~~{.Bash} $ pandoc --version pandoc 2.18 $ echo '[Foo bar](https://example.com){.class1 .class1}' | pandoc -w html

Foo bar

$ echo '[Foo bar](https://example.com){.class1 .class1 .class1 .class1 .class1 .class1 .class1}' | pandoc -w html

Foo bar

~~~ So probably what happened with my 733+ ``s with duplicate classes is that as my various documents roundtrip through Pandoc in various ways, whether being generated originally or written & read or munged through the API, the table rows get marked up as even/odd for zebra-striping styling, and each time, the even/odd code simply chucks another class onto the `` without checking if it's necessary; and the writer then just passes that through, so the number builds up. This presumably applies to other elements that Pandoc will write classes on and all other ways classes might get added. --- This is a minor style/reliability issue, and not a serious bug: the HTML standards do not forbid duplicate classes, so it's legal/valid, and it will not in and of itself cause any bugs, because browsers will just collapse any number of `class1` instances into a single `class1` (it's idempotent / treated as a set). However, I think it is worth fixing: it is widely considered a HTML lint issue and best practices is to eliminate duplicates\*; it leads to confusion while debugging; it makes the source less readable if you have to remember that all the varying instances are the same thing; it makes editing harder (more to remove/edit); and it wastes a few bytes. The cost of a fix is low: while one could add checks to everything that messes with classes, it'd be easier to fix it in the writer at the final stage - it's just the class field of an `Attr`, so it's presumably localized to a single line; there should be no regressions or API changes involved as all downstream tools should be interpreting duplicate classes as a single class per the standards; performance-wise, most classes are null, so no uniquing is necessary at all; most non-null classes are just 1 class (like the tables in question would just be `class="even"` or `class="odd"`), so likewise; and most other classes will be so short that the cost of something like a `nub` would be unmeasurable (especially if Pandoc is no longer generating duplicate classes). --- On a side note, I seem to recall already reporting this issue, but I couldn't refind my report, and I think I might've been confusing it with a different HTML lint issue? If I did already report this exact issue, my apologies. \* To quote an authority no less impeachable than GPT-4 itself on the matter of why to remove duplicate HTML classes: :) > 1. Clean and maintainable code: Having duplicate redundant classes makes the HTML code messy and harder to maintain. Ensuring that there are no duplicate classes improves the readability of the code and makes it easier for developers to understand and update. > 2. Performance: Although the performance impact may be minimal, removing duplicate classes can help reduce the file size of the HTML and CSS code, leading to faster loading times for the website. > 3. Debugging: Duplicate classes can make it difficult to debug and troubleshoot styling issues. Removing duplicates helps to isolate issues and resolve them more quickly. > 4. Best practices: Ensuring that there are no duplicate classes on an HTML element is a best practice in web development, and adhering to best practices results in better quality code and a more professional outcome. > 5. Avoid conflicts: Duplicate classes can potentially cause conflicts when using CSS frameworks or third-party libraries, which might have their own styles applied to the same class names. Removing duplicates helps to avoid these conflicts. > 6. Accessibility: Ensuring a clean and well-structured HTML code, including avoiding duplicate classes

title: [ext req] Syntax for image (figure) caption vs alt
body:
I found these relevant issues:
- https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/issues/4737 discusses the ability to have both caption and alt
- https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/issues/3177 implements it

And these relevant forum discussions:
- [Image with separate alt-text and caption?](https://groups.google.com/g/pandoc-discuss/c/BefkPmp0x84/m/6HSogH5EAQAJ) discusses the ability
- [The difference between image caption and title](https://groups.google.com/g/pandoc-discuss/c/ODzdD-nGZbs/m/n8lr9mrQAQAJ) poses a latex question, but is not answered

None of the above discusses which is alt, and which is caption.
There seems to be some confusion:
- https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#images gives two examples, 
```
![la lune](lalune.jpg "Voyage to the moon")  # caption in quotes?
![This is the caption](/url/of/image.png)    # caption in brackets?
```
The pandoc HTML exporter implements "caption in brackets".

The problem is that the emacs orgmode exporters (markdown and HTML) implement "caption in quotes", i.e.
```
![Alt text](/path/to/img.jpg)
![Alt text](/path/to/img.jpg "Optional title")
```

You can see this in discussion [[BUG] ox-md image captions](https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/emacs-orgmode/2023-04/threads.html#00055).
According to the implementor of `ox-md`, this is the behavior as specified in the following specs:
- Original MD: https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax#img
- CommonMark https://spec.commonmark.org/0.30/#images

As for GFM:
- https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax#images shows only "brackets"
- But a quick test shows that text in brackets is not shown, whereas text in "quotes" is shown as a tooltip over the image:
![alt text](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/536250/230128015-8880e740-e552-4396-9292-fb140f57e417.png "caption text")


From reading https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/issues/4737, I assume there's no way Pandoc will change its default behavior because that would be disruptive?
I proposed an Org export option, but the org developers countered that it makes more sense for Pandoc to have an import option, because ox-md is "spec compliant".

So can we have an extension `figure_caption_vs_alt` that swaps the current behavior?

title: Default to prettyfied output of native format for `pandoc lua -i`
body:
With `pandoc` we get nice indented native syntax
````
> pandoc -f markdown -t native
![My Image](local/img/jpg)
^Z
[ Figure
    ( "" , [] , [] )
    (Caption
       Nothing [ Plain [ Str "My" , Space , Str "Image" ] ])
    [ Plain
        [ Image
            ( "" , [] , [] )
            [ Str "My" , Space , Str "Image" ]
            ( "local/img/jpg" , "" )
        ]
    ]
]
````
but with `pandoc lua -i` we don't 
````
> pandoc lua -i
Lua 5.4.4  Copyright (C) 1994-2022 Lua.org, PUC-Rio
Embedded in pandoc 3.1.2
> pandoc.Figure( pandoc.Image( {}, 'local/img.jpg'),  { 'My image' })
Figure ("",[],[]) (Caption Nothing [Plain [Str "My",Space,Str "image"]]) [Plain [Image ("",[],[]) [] ("local/img.jpg","")]] 
````

It seems it would be worth doing the same indented output for easier reading, especially with interactive usage. maybe using a flag like `pandoc lua --pretty -i` to opt-in (or a flag to opt out) if we want to keep concise form.

title: Spurious errors working with pandoc defaults file due to LSP
body:
When using the yaml-lsp and working on a defaults file, you get a lot of spurious errors from the LSP:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/73286100/234591662-f1533484-3b2b-4898-ba93-7bffd2fa7c5d.png)

these diagnostics are all completely false, since the defaults file is working fine. 

I did some digging and figured out that those are caused by an unfortunate chain of dependencies:
- the yaml-lsp generates diagnostics for yaml files based on the on schemas. 
- These schemas are sourced from the [schemastore](https://www.schemastore.org/). The schema store in turn sources (some) of their schemas from external providers.
- one such provider is ansible. In particular, the [ansible-lint repo](https://github.com/ansible/ansible-lint/issues/3341) hosts a schema for [ansible vars file](https://github.com/ansible/ansible-lint/blob/main/src/ansiblelint/schemas/vars.json). One of the patterns used to identify a file as ansible vars file is `"defaults/*.yml"`
- this pattern results in the yaml-lsp recognizing any yaml file located in a `defaults` subdirectory as an ansible file and applies its patterns there.

Now coincidentally, "defaults" is also exactly the name of the directory in your pandoc `--data-dir`, where your defaults files have to be stored when you do not keep them in your working directory:
> All options for document conversion, including input and output files, can be set using a defaults file. The file will be searched for first in the working directory, and then in the defaults subdirectory of the user data directory ([pandoc docs](https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#option--data-dir))

The result are spurious errors by the LSP, even if you do not work with ansible files at all. Annoyingly you also cannot work around as end user, since the yaml LSP does only allow to *change* schemas for a file, but does not allow you to *disable* schemas for a file: https://github.com/redhat-developer/yaml-language-server/issues/446

---

Since the problem lies somewhere in between yaml-ls, schemastore, ansible, and pandoc, I created corresponding issues as well, with no luck (for now):
- the ansible folks state that they use the file only for their test-suite. (which for whatever reason ended up being fed to the yaml-ls apparently?) They state that you (pandoc) should use a more specific naming convention/pattern for pandoc default files: https://github.com/ansible/ansible-lint/issues/3341
- the issue I created at the schemastore repo has resulted in any response yet: https://github.com/SchemaStore/schemastore/issues/2919
- at the yaml-ls repo, the bug report form strongly emphasizes that issues with schemas should not be reported there but rather at the schema provider

Note that while this problem is created by a convergence of decisions from multiple projects, the end result – the spurious errors – are not an edge case, they apparently appear for *all* pandoc user working with yaml defaults files and using the yaml-lsp.

---

**possible solutions I can think of**
- hope that the schema store might change something on their end
- creation of a schema for pandoc defaults files that can either be used manually or submitted to the schemastore
- changing the naming pattern/convention for pandoc default's files as the ansible people suggested
